summary: Defines how the 6bone IPv6 test network used its test address prefix to create pseudo top-level and next-level aggregation identifiers. It is informational and applied only to that experimental network.

plainLanguage.summary: The 6bone was a practice network for a new kind of Internet address. This explains how it carved up its practice addresses.

questions: what is a ptla in ipv6
subtitle: How the 6bone IPv6 testbed divided up its test address space

tldr.problem: The 6bone (an IPv6 testbed network) needed to divide a single test address prefix into hierarchical zones for different backbone networks and their downward delegations, similar to how real IPv6 would be deployed.
tldr.mechanism: Create pseudo Top-Level Aggregation identifiers (pTLAs) as the first tier and pseudo Next-Level Aggregation identifiers (pNLAs) as the second tier within the 3FFE::/16 test prefix, with two format versions designed at different times to accommodate network growth.
tldr.outcome: The 6bone was able to grow from supporting 256 backbone networks to supporting thousands, providing a realistic testbed for IPv6 address hierarchy before production IPv6 deployment.

today: RFC 2921 is an Informational document specific to the 6bone, which was shut down in June 2006. It remains a historical record of how the testbed managed its IPv6 address space during IPv6 development. The 6bone's experience with hierarchical address delegation influenced the design of real-world IPv6 address allocation policies.

sections.title: IPv6 Testing and the 6bone
sections.content:
The 6bone was an early testbed network used to test IPv6 specifications and implementations before real IPv6 deployment. To avoid consuming precious real IPv6 address space, the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) reserved a single 16-bit test prefix, 3FFE::/16, allocated in RFC 2471 for this purpose.

However, 3FFE::/16 is just one TLA block. To create a realistic prototype of how real IPv6 address delegation would work, the 6bone needed to define how to subdivide this prefix into pseudo Top-Level Aggregation identifiers (pTLAs) and pseudo Next-Level Aggregation identifiers (pNLAs), mimicking the structure specified in RFC 2374 for production IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The 6bone got one big practice address range from the global registry. They had to figure out how to chop it up into smaller pieces for different organizations, like how the real Internet divides addresses.

sections.title: Original 8-bit pTLA and 24-bit pNLA Format
sections.content:
The original pTLA/pNLA design used 8 bits for the pTLA and 24 bits for the pNLA. This provided 256 possible pTLAs (i.e., 256 different backbone networks), each with 24 bits of NLA space available for their own downward delegations. In prefix notation, a pTLA block is written as 3FFE:nn00::/24, where nn is the 8-bit pTLA assignment.

Each pTLA provider could then assign bits from their 24-bit pNLA space to organizations below them, creating a hierarchical multi-level delegation similar to real IPv6. For example, a provider could reserve some pNLA bits for direct customer sites and delegate further bits to intermediate transit ISPs.
sections.plainLanguage: The original plan gave each backbone network (pTLA) 256 possible addresses, and each backbone network could split those addresses among their own customers however they wanted.

sections.title: Extended 12-bit pTLA and 20-bit pNLA Format
sections.content:
After the 6bone began supporting multiple purposes (transition experimentation in addition to specification testing), it became clear that 256 pTLAs would not be enough. In 1999, the community defined a new format using 12 bits for the pTLA and 20 bits for the pNLA. This design provides up to 4096 pTLAs but starts new allocations at 3FFE:0x800::/28 (value 0x800 and above), preserving the original 8-bit pTLAs in the lower range for backward compatibility.

The new pTLA is written as 3FFE:nnn0::/28, where nnn is the 12-bit pTLA assignment. The remaining 20-bit pNLA space per pTLA allows for continued hierarchical delegation similar to the original design.
sections.plainLanguage: When they realized 256 backbones wasn't enough, they switched to a bigger system that could handle up to 4,000 backbones, while keeping the old addresses still working.

sections.title: Hierarchical Delegation Example
sections.content:
An example workflow under the new format: assume a pTLA assignment of 0x800 (a backbone network) with no intermediate ISP (pNLA1 of 0x00) and a site identifier of 0x0001. The resulting routing prefix would be 3FFE:8000:0001::/48. Alternatively, if an intermediate transit ISP (pNLA1 of 0x80) sits between the backbone and a customer with the same site ID, the address becomes 3FFE:0180:0001::/48. Note that the two sites numbered 0x0001 are different because their pNLA1 providers differ.

This hierarchical structure matches real IPv6 address allocation principles, where each tier can delegate authority downward to the next level.
sections.plainLanguage: Different parts of the practice network could be split and re-split, creating branches and sub-branches of organization, just like in the real Internet.

sections.title: Registry and Documentation
sections.content:
The 6bone maintains a RIPE-style registry database to document all IPv6 sites and address allocations connected to the testbed. The registry includes an inet6num object that allows complete documentation of all IPv6 addresses allocated in the 6bone. This registry serves as the authoritative source for tracking which organizations hold which address blocks.

The address format definitions enable any network tool to parse a 6bone address and determine its hierarchical origin without needing to query the registry for every address seen.
sections.plainLanguage: There's a database that keeps track of who got which address pieces, so nobody accidentally uses the same address twice.
